issues.explanation: The profile is for a 61-year-old bus driver who witnessed trauma. 'Bicycle' as a trigger is not impossible, but in combination with the rest of the profile it points toward a very specific accident scenario that is not supported elsewhere in the report. The other items emphasize guilt, sensory reliving, and contamination/interpersonal avoidance, creating a mixed picture that is hard to unify around a single witnessed-trauma account.

issues.explanation: Feeling 'dirty or contaminated' is much more characteristic of sexual or contact-based interpersonal trauma than of witnessed trauma. For a witnessed-trauma formulation, this appraisal is difficult to reconcile unless there was direct bodily involvement, which is not reflected elsewhere.

Avoiding sex is hard to explain from the rest of this profile. The selected memory and appraisal items center on reliving and guilt about inaction, but do not support a coherent mechanism for sexual avoidance in a witnessed-trauma case.

vignette:
María is a 61-year-old bus driver for the city transit authority, married for thirty-seven years to a retired warehouse worker. The event that undid her occurred two years ago, on a humid September afternoon. She was driving her usual route through a busy intersection when a sedan ran a red light and struck a woman crossing the street. María remembers the sound—a wet, crunching thump—and the way the woman’s body folded under the bumper. She stopped the bus, ran out, and knelt beside the victim, who was bleeding heavily from a head wound. María had taken a first-aid course years ago, but in the moment her hands froze; she could not recall a single step. The woman died before the ambulance arrived. That image—the blood pooling on the asphalt, the woman’s open, unseeing eyes—lodged in María’s mind like a splinter. She has not been able to remove it since. Because the memory came back so vividly, ordinary sounds — a car door slamming, a radio crackling — began to feel like warnings she could not ignore, each one carrying the potential to pull her back into that intersection. To keep the memory from surfacing while she drove, she began reciting a silent countdown under her breath each time she turned the ignition, a ritual she hoped would crowd the image out.

In the weeks that followed, María found herself avoiding physical contact with anyone. When her husband touched her shoulder, she flinched. She stopped letting passengers brush past her, standing rigidly at the front of the bus, gripping the wheel. The sight of blood—even a nosebleed on a child’s shirt—would send a wave of shame through her: I did nothing. I let her die. That sense of failure took root. She began to believe her life was no longer worth living, though she never said it aloud. She secretly performed mental rituals—counting backward from a hundred in Spanish under her breath every time she started the engine, repeating no more, no more until it felt safe to drive. She hoped these acts would prevent another accident, but they never fully quieted the guilt.

The memory itself refused to stay in the past. Sometimes, while sitting at a red light, María would suddenly smell the hot asphalt and hear the thump again, every sense alive as if she were back on that street corner. Other times, the emotion would hit her without any image—a crushing despair that came from nowhere, leaving her gasping. She was certain that if she had acted faster, the woman would have survived; that conviction made the memory feel like it was happening right now, not two years ago. That conviction also meant that even the most routine situation — a car slowing, a pedestrian hesitating — now registered as a sign that she was about to fail again, so she could not afford to look away. That guilt, in turn, sharpened her attention to any car that drifted close to a crosswalk. She began scanning intersections with a fierce vigilance, looking for anyone about to be hit. The bus depot’s TV reporting a fender bender would send her heart racing.

Her avoidance grew more elaborate. She switched her route to one that bypassed the intersection entirely, taking longer to get home. But the longer route became its own reminder: every detour was a daily acknowledgement of what she was avoiding, and the memory rose more insistently with each mile. She asked her husband not to mention the victim’s name—she had learned it was Dolores—and turned off the radio when a news segment about pedestrian deaths came on. But the rituals did not hold. Counting backward sometimes triggered a vivid replay of the scene. The avoidance itself reminded her that she was still afraid, still failing to move on. Each time she flinched at a touch, she felt a fresh wave of self-reproach: I am a coward. I could not help her, and now I cannot even let my own husband hold my hand. The mental rituals, intended to give her control, only reinforced her sense that she had none. She started to believe that if she stopped the counting, someone else would die.

After more than a year, her husband gently told her he missed her, that she seemed like a ghost. That same week, she saw a memorial cross at the intersection where Dolores died, and she broke down in tears at the wheel, unable to drive the bus for the rest of her shift. Her supervisor suggested she take leave. María finally agreed to see a therapist because she could no longer bear the weight of the memory—or the thought that she might harm someone else through her own paralysis. She came to the first session hesitant, her hands folded in her lap, and said quietly, “I think I stopped living the day she died. I just don’t know how to start again.” What frightens her most is that the counting will stop working, and she will be left with nothing but the blood and the guilt.

violations.explanation: The vignette does not show that negative appraisals cause or amplify triggers; rather, triggers lead to appraisals.
The vignette does not show the memory directly causing avoidance or rituals; maladaptive strategies are driven by appraisals, not directly by memory.
The vignette does not show the memory itself creating or increasing sensitivity to triggers.
The vignette does not show maladaptive strategies (avoidance, rituals) leading to the emergence or intensification of triggers.

vignette_attempts.feedback:
REQUIRED EDGES MISSING:
- Negative Appraisals → Triggers: The vignette does not show that negative appraisals cause or amplify triggers; rather, triggers lead to appraisals.
  e.g. "Once she had concluded that the world was fundamentally unsafe, almost anything could confirm it — a figure in her periphery, the wrong tone of voice, footsteps behind her."
  e.g. "The belief that she couldn't trust her own judgement meant that things she would once have registered and dismissed now snagged and held her attention."
  e.g. "Her conviction that it would happen again meant she moved through ordinary days as if they were mined — every ambiguity became a potential signal."
- Memory → Maladaptive Strategies: The vignette does not show the memory directly causing avoidance or rituals; maladaptive strategies are driven by appraisals, not directly by memory.
  e.g. "She had learned that if she kept the television on loud enough, the thoughts couldn't get a foothold — silence was the enemy."
  e.g. "After the memory surfaced during sex, she began finding quiet reasons to avoid intimacy altogether, telling herself she was simply tired or stressed."
  e.g. "To stop the images coming at night, she started staying up later and later, until exhaustion was the only reliable way to fall asleep."
- Memory → Triggers: The vignette does not show the memory itself creating or increasing sensitivity to triggers.
  e.g. "After the memory had surfaced, even the most ordinary things — a kettle whistling, a door slamming — felt like warnings she couldn't afford to ignore."
  e.g. "The intrusive image left her scanning every room she entered, cataloguing exits, tracking faces, unable to switch off."
  e.g. "Because the memory came back so vividly, she began to see threads of it everywhere: in strangers' faces, in certain times of day, in the quality of winter light."
- Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers: The vignette does not show maladaptive strategies (avoidance, rituals) leading to the emergence or intensification of triggers.
  e.g. "Each place she avoided became a reminder in itself — the long way round she walked every morning was its own daily acknowledgement of what had happened."
  e.g. "Her safety behaviours had drawn a map of the event around her: everything she couldn't do, everywhere she couldn't go, every person she kept at arm's length."
  e.g. "The avoidance had grown in all directions until the city was full of routes she no longer used and things she could no longer say."
